**Y components**
- **Y3 = bit 4.** In X1‑Y3‑Z3, yellow appears exactly when bit 4 is 1 in both stimuli.
- **Y2 = bit 1.** In X5‑Y2‑Z3 and X5‑Y2‑Z1, the rare button appears exactly when bit 1 is 1 in both stimuli.
- **Y4 = bit 2.** In X4‑Y4‑Z2, blue appears exactly when bit 2 is 0 in both stimuli. X6‑Y4‑Z2 then splits cleanly on whether the two bit‑2 values are the same.

**X and Z components: two families fit all the examples**

| | X1 | X5 | Z3 (true / false) |
|---|---|---|---|
| (i) | both are 1 | not both are 1 | yellow / blue |
| (ii) | not both are 1 | both are 1 | blue / yellow |

| | X3 | X6 | X4 | Z2 (true / false) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | exactly one is 1 | both are the same | at least one is 1 | red / blue |
| (b) | both are the same | exactly one is 1 | neither is 1 | blue / red |

Every one of the 4 combinations fits all six known tasks, and all X versions stay distinct.

**What this means for X1‑Y3‑Z2**
The new task depends only on whether bit 4 is 1 in both stimuli. The combinations disagree about the colour:
- (i)+(a) and (ii)+(b): both‑1 → red, otherwise blue.
- (i)+(b) and (ii)+(a): both‑1 → blue, otherwise red.

So the examples do not determine the answers. I chose X1 = "both are 1", which matches its position first in the rule list, and Z2 = "true → red". Under that choice, bit 4 is 1 in both stimuli only in inputs 4, 6 and 9, so those are red and all others are blue.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: blue, yellow, green, or red. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> green` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is green.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
